triage_context.environment: Internet-facing web service (HTTP is untrusted). Reachability judged against the intended public deployment in the README (DigitalOcean App Platform, open public signup, SPA served same-origin), not against the app currently running only on a developer machine.
threat_model: Code execution in a visitor's browser
Loss or tampering of user content
triage_context.scoring: Derived HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW from preconditions and access level
triage_context.fp_rules: .claude/fp-rules.txt (6 org exclusions O1-O6 plus 3 explicit still-reportable carve-outs)
caveats: Phase 4 severity was derived inline by the orchestrator rather than by per-finding ranking subagents: an Anthropic session limit blocked further agent spawns. It applies the skill's precondition rule to preconditions the Phase-3 verifiers established.
f013 was never verified - all three of its verifiers were killed by the same session limit. It is carried as needs_manual_test under the recall policy, not because analysis was inconclusive.

findings.title: Upload filename takes its extension from the client, and the file is served back from the application origin
preconditions: Attacker holds any verified account (open signup, so effectively free)
Victim opens the uploaded file's URL directly - the SPA renders photos in an , where .html/.svg will not execute, so the attacker must distribute the app-origin link
findings.threat_match: Code execution in a visitor's browser
findings.rationale:
file_uploud.js:10 takes the stored extension from client-controlled file.originalname, and the sole gate at file_uploud.js:18 tests file.mimetype, which is the client-written multipart Content-Type rather than a byte-derived type - a grep of the tree shows no magic-byte or extension allowlist anywhere. The file is served same-origin by routes/recipe.js:281 via res.sendFile with no options, so Express sets Content-Type: text/html for a .html upload, and index.js sets no CSP or X-Content-Type-Options. The uploader learns the URL because recipe.js:68 stores /data/recipes_pics/<recipeId>.<ext> and recipe.js:78 returns recipe_id, and the serving route is unauthenticated. Org rule O6 expressly leaves the inbound naming/typing of uploads reportable.

Authenticated-only and needing the victim to open the link caps the raw derivation at MEDIUM, but the account barrier is nominal and the delivery step is a normal-looking same-origin URL. Boosted one step on the operator's 'code execution in a visitor's browser' threat. SCANNER CORRECTION: the original exploit scenario's document.cookie exfiltration does not work - session_config.js:25 sets httpOnly. Impact is undiminished because the payload can drive authenticated same-origin fetch (delete the victim's recipes, read /api/recipes/mine, post as them).
findings.owner_hint: component: file_uploud.js; no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer jozoforza (3/4 recent commits); serving side routes/recipe.js is smacica (10/15)

findings.title: Account takeover: Google sign-in links to a pre-registered local account and marks it verified
preconditions: Attacker registers the victim's email address via the open signup route BEFORE the victim's first Google sign-in (db.js:576 refuses an already-taken address, so the ordering is strict)
The victim subsequently signs in with Google at least once
findings.rationale:
db.js:554 sets email_verified = 1 on any pre-existing row matched only by email (db.js:549, dbFindByEmail is a plain LOWER(email) match at db.js:471) and never clears password, so an attacker-created local row from the unauthenticated /api/signup (routes/user.js:44, inserted email_verified: false with an attacker-chosen bcrypt hash via db.js:585) becomes sign-inable the moment the real owner authenticates with Google. local_strategy.js:30 gates local sign-in solely on email_verified, and bcrypt.compare at local_strategy.js:25 matches the attacker's own password, so the intended dbConsumeEmailToken proof-of-ownership path (db.js:500-526) is bypassed entirely. profile.emails[0].verified is additionally never consulted (google_strategy.js:25).

Two preconditions caps the raw derivation at MEDIUM, but both are cheap: signup is open and unrated, and the second is simply the victim using the product as intended. The threat-model boost applies squarely - this is the operator's first-named unacceptable outcome - taking it to HIGH.
findings.owner_hint: component: db.js (auth/identity layer); no CODEOWNERS entry; top committers smacica (8/16) and jozoforza (8/16) - split ownership, route to both

findings.title: OAuth flow omits the state parameter, allowing login CSRF
preconditions: Attacker obtains an unspent Google authorization code for their own account (free - signup is open)
Victim's browser is induced to visit the callback URL within the code's ~10-minute validity window
findings.threat_match: Loss or tampering of user content (one-step boost deliberately not applied)
findings.rationale:
google_strategy.js:13-19 omits state/store, and both authenticate calls (routes/user.js:138, routes/user.js:146) omit it too, so passport-oauth2/lib/strategy.js:113 installs a NullStore whose verify in lib/state/null.js returns cb(null, true) unconditionally - the callback at routes/user.js:145 accepts any well-formed code from any browser with zero session binding. A project-wide grep finds no state or CSRF handling anywhere, and routes/user.js:157 does not require req.session.returnTo to have been set, so an unsolicited callback is not rejected. The sameSite: 'lax' cookie is still sent on the top-level GET navigation - the comment at session_config.js:26 says so explicitly - so req.login at routes/user.js:152 writes the attacker's identity into the victim's session.

Bounded because db.js:542 never consults req.user, so the attacker cannot link their identity onto a victim's live session. A threat-model match exists but the one-step boost is deliberately NOT applied: all three verifiers independently judged MEDIUM correct for this impact.
findings.owner_hint: component: google_strategy.js; no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer smacica (2/2 recent commits - sole author)

findings.title: CORS reflects any Origin with credentials enabled
preconditions: CLIENT_URL is empty in production - the README's explicit instruction
Attacker controls an origin that is same-SITE with the deployment (a sibling subdomain), OR the operator later sets sameSite:'none' to split the SPA onto its own origin
Victim visits that origin while holding a live session
findings.rationale:
index.js:43-44 passes origin: clientUrl || true, credentials: true, and clientUrl is empty in the documented production config (index.js:22, README.md:213-217), so cors 2.8.5 takes the reflect branch at node_modules/cors/lib/index.js:57-66 and emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <attacker origin> with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true - verified in the library source, not assumed. Honestly assessed, sameSite: 'lax' (session_config.js:27) does blunt the headline scenario: a conforming browser withholds connect.sid on a cross-site fetch, so isLoggedIn returns 401 and the attacker reads nothing authenticated from attacker.tld today. It remains real because Lax is same-site, not same-origin: any subdomain foothold gets the cookie attached, and index.js:43 is then the sole control preventing it reading /api/profile's email, while app.options('*') pre-clears non-simple credentialed methods on every path.

Three preconditions derives LOW; the PII threat match lifts it to MEDIUM. Mitigated by SameSite=Lax - but that control is incidental (chosen for the OAuth redirect), site-scoped rather than origin-scoped, and the only thing standing in the way.
findings.owner_hint: component: index.js (app wiring); no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer smacica (8/14 recent commits)

findings.title: Verification links are built from the Host header when PUBLIC_URL is unset
preconditions: PUBLIC_URL is empty in production - the shipped default, and absent from the README's production env block
The platform ingress forwards a request carrying an unrecognised Host rather than rejecting it (DigitalOcean routes by Host; unverifiable from source)
Victim clicks the confirmation button in the mail, which the mail explicitly asks them to do
findings.rationale:
routes/user.js:19 feeds the raw req.get('host') header into issueVerificationEmail at routes/user.js:53 and :123, both unauthenticated routes, and local_strategy.js:46 concatenates it with a live verification token that mailer.js:27 mails as a clickable href. The only mitigation is the optional PUBLIC_URL, which fails open and ships empty in both .env.example:18 and the operator's actual .env; app.set('trust proxy', 1) governs req.ip/req.protocol, not the Host header the code reads - one verifier confirmed against installed Express 4.18.2 (node_modules/express/lib/request.js:427-449) that the X-Forwarded-Host logic lives only on req.hostname. Replaying the stolen token at db.js:500-526 verifies the account, and db.js:553 later merges the victim's Google sign-in into that attacker-controlled row.

Three preconditions drops the raw derivation to LOW; the account-takeover match lifts it one step. Two of three verifiers argued HIGH was overstated on impact too: dbConsumeEmailToken only sets email_verified and never calls req.login, so a stolen token grants no session - the real outcomes are service-authentic phishing and account pre-hijacking that chains with f001. needs_manual_test because precondition 2 is a platform behaviour no amount of source reading can settle.
findings.owner_hint: component: routes/user.js; no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer smacica (6/10 recent commits)

findings.title: Session signing secret silently falls back to a hardcoded literal
preconditions: Operator deploys with SESSION_SECRET unset or misspelled - reachable via the README's own cp .env.example .env flow, since .env.example ships the variable empty and '' is falsy
Attacker knows the literal, which is published in this repository
findings.rationale:
session_config.js:22 is verbatim `secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET || "dev-only-secret"` with only a logger.warn at session_config.js:11-13, and the config is mounted unconditionally at index.js:47, so a deployment missing the variable serves public traffic signed with a repo-published key. The claimed exploitation path is a misread - the store is server-side (session_config.js:23; express-sqlite3 get() returns undefined for unknown sids), sids are UUIDv4, and passport@0.6.0 regenerates the session inside req.login (routes/user.js:82, :152), so a forged cookie yields an anonymous session rather than an account. The underlying defect is real and explicitly in scope per org rules, so the verdict holds while the HIGH severity does not.

All three verifiers independently reached the same correction and unanimously recommended downgrading to MEDIUM and rewriting the description before it reaches an engineer. Controls reducing it: server-side session store, uuid v4 ids, login-time regeneration.
findings.owner_hint: component: session_config.js; no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer jozoforza (3/5 recent commits)

findings.title: Email format regex runs against an unbounded request string
preconditions: UNVERIFIED - no verifier completed. Claimed: attacker POSTs a large crafted email field to the unauthenticated signup route, bounded by the 100 kB body-parser limit
findings.rationale:
NOT VERIFIED. All three verifier agents were terminated by an Anthropic session limit before producing a verdict, and a retry was impossible because the limit had not reset. Per the tally rule, three unparseable votes count as cannot_verify, yielding no majority; under the operator's chosen recall policy that is carried forward as true_positive/needs_manual_test rather than dropped. Nothing here reflects an analytical judgment - it reflects an infrastructure failure. The underlying claim is unchanged: looksLikeEmail tests /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/ (routes/user.js:23) against String(req.body.email || '').trim() (routes/user.js:33) with no length cap, bounded only by the 100 kB body-parser limit (index.js:48).

Carried at the scanner's own LOW rather than derived, because it would be dishonest to rank on an unexamined claim. A human should settle it by timing the regex against a 100 kB crafted input; the fix is a length cap either way and costs nothing.
findings.owner_hint: component: routes/user.js; no CODEOWNERS entry; top committer smacica (6/10 recent commits)

findings.title: Verification links are printed to stdout when SMTP is not configured
findings.rationale: The console.log at mailer.js:39 is real and reachable indirectly from unauthenticated POST /api/signup (routes/user.js:53) and POST /api/resend-verification (routes/user.js:123), but the printed token is not an account credential: dbConsumeEmailToken (db.js:500-526) only runs UPDATE users SET email_verified = 1 (db.js:517), and the redeeming route routes/user.js:98-114 never calls req.login - unlike routes/user.js:82 and :152 - so redemption grants no session, and no password-reset flow exists in the repo. The fallback fires only when an operator leaves SMTP_* unset, a state that warns at boot (mailer.js:7-9), is documented verbatim in README.md:94-103, is surfaced to clients as delivered:false, and is explicitly carved out by test/no_console.test.js:9-14. No HTTP route reads or serves logs. Two refinements the scanner missed: the pre-hijack chain is blocked because dbCreateLocalUser returns null on a taken address (db.js:576-579), and 'misconfigured' SMTP does not reach this branch at all - only fully-absent config does.

findings.title: Query helpers interpolate table, column and LIMIT into SQL text
findings.rationale: Every call site of dbFind, dbUpdate and dbDel passes string literals for table/column and only 1 or 'all' for limit; dbUpdate/dbDel are imported by no module outside db.js and dbDel has zero call sites. The sole variable identifier, rankComlumn[0]/[1] at db.js:165/176/177/193, is assigned from hardcoded arrays at db.js:144/146 with a hard reject at db.js:150, and its untrusted entry point routes/recipe.js:266 is gated by `like !== 0 && like !== 1` at recipe.js:262. Request-derived values reach only bound ? parameters. Org rule O1 requires a request-derived value to actually reach a table, column or limit argument - no such path exists, making this a latent footgun rather than a vulnerability. All three verifiers independently enumerated every call site and agreed at confidence 9.

findings.title: Recipe ids truncate a UUID to 32 bits, and the id also names the uploaded photo
findings.rationale: The truncation is real - parseInt(uuid(),16) at routes/recipe.js:37 yields 32 random bits, and multer names the photo from it before the recipe_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY INSERT can reject a duplicate. But the id is not a secret: routes/recipe.js:287 serves every recipe_id and photo path unauthenticated, and deletion is ownership-gated inside db.js:270, so guessability grants nothing. The only concrete impact, a photo overwrite, requires the server to independently draw a colliding CSPRNG value the attacker cannot influence - 1-in-2^32 for a chosen target - with a random thumbnail swap as the payoff, and no stored-XSS escalation because the overwrite only lands when the extension already matches. Real reliability defect (collisions reach ~1% at 10k recipes), but file it as robustness, not security.

findings.title: safeNext accepts backslash-prefixed paths that browsers resolve as protocol-relative
findings.rationale: safeNext (routes/user.js:14) genuinely fails to reject /\, but the tainted value cannot reach the sink: req.login at routes/user.js:152 passes no options, so passport 0.6.0's sessionmanager.js:28 regenerates the session and express-session/session/store.js:50-56 destroys it and installs a blank Session - leaving req.session.returnTo undefined when routes/user.js:157 reads it, so safeNext(undefined) returns '/'. The only two safeNext call sites are inside /auth/google and /auth/google/callback, the precise routes org rule O5 excludes from open-redirect reporting. Worth a one-line hardening fix because a passport upgrade or keepSessionInfo:true would arm it, but not a live vulnerability.

findings.title: Vote endpoint passes an unparsed path parameter to the data layer without an existence check
findings.rationale: recipe.js:266 really does forward the raw string, but likes.recipe_id has INTEGER affinity (db.js:46), so SQLite applies numeric affinity to the no-affinity bound parameter at db.js:155 and converts integral text on insert at db.js:189 - '42' and 42 are indistinguishable, refuting the affinity claim. The orphan-row claim fails because the FK rejects the INSERT, and PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON at db.js:120 does take effect: node-sqlite3 prepares every statement via sqlite3_prepare_v2 on one shared connection handle, and SQLite sets flag pragmas at compile time, so db.get versus db.run is immaterial. The scanner's own open question was answered decisively against the finding. Worth a cleanup to return 400/404 instead of 500, but no security consequence.

findings.title: dbDel's two-column branch builds a SELECT and runs it as the delete
findings.rationale: The mechanical claim is correct - db.js:646-647 overwrites the DELETE with a SELECT that db.run executes and resolves successfully. But dbDel has zero callers: it appears only at its definition and export, all six importers destructure explicit name lists omitting it, and there is no whole-module import or dynamic access. Decisively, the very failure the finding hypothesizes - a future caller invalidating an email token and resolving without revoking it - is already implemented correctly elsewhere, at db.js:484 and db.js:510, neither of which touches dbDel. A genuine footgun worth a cleanup ticket (fix the branch or delete the helper along with the other unused exports addLike and dbRecipes), but not a security finding.
